summary:
Oyo State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies in full to visitors. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Oyo is a southern state governed by the Criminal Code, which separately penalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. Oyo lies outside the Shari'a regime; twelve northern states (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara) apply Shari'a law, under which male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death.

Police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay, a practice known locally as 'kito'. Mass arrests recur across Nigeria: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. No anti-discrimination protections exist.

The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, and LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that applies in full to Oyo.

Criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular dating apps, entrap men, film them, then extort, beat and kidnap them. A BBC Africa Eye investigation (15 May 2023) interviewed 21 people about being 'kito'd'. Victims do not report to police for fear of being arrested or attacked. The investigation also showed enforcement against the gangs, including a commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. The underground scene described is Lagos-based, while the risk of dating-app 'kito' extortion applies to gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria.
tangentialFactors:
The Shari'a regime in twelve northern states, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death, does not apply in Oyo; visitors crossing into those states face a materially different and more severe legal exposure.

Mass-arrest figures cited for Nigeria (Lagos, Kaduna, Delta, Warri, Gombe) are raw counts from other states and do not measure Oyo-specific enforcement.
localsOnly:
Residents of Oyo State face the Criminal Code penalties for sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years) alongside the SSMPA's penalties, with no anti-discrimination protection in place.

LGBTI organisations in Oyo fall within the reach of the 2014 statute's prohibition on registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations.

Police practice of profiling, entrapment and extortion of people perceived as gay ('kito') affects residents as well as visitors, and victims commonly do not report resulting crimes to police.
outOfScopeNotes:
Oyo-specific arrest, prosecution and violence figures are not present in the source inventory; the mass-arrest counts cited are from other Nigerian states and are reported as national-pattern evidence only.

The extent of enforcement against transgender residents of Oyo, and any Oyo-specific incidents involving trans people, is not sourced here.

Whether Oyo State has issued any state-level directives on cross-dressing or gender presentation is unresolved in the available sources.
